claims.text: Coexisting electrochemically dissimilar phases in a eutectic high-entropy alloy create localized micro-galvanic cells.
Mechanical wear at elevated temperature accelerates removal of protective oxide layers.
Micro-galvanic coupling causes preferential corrosion of the more anodic phase.
Feedback between wear-induced surface exposure and galvanic corrosion synergistically increases both wear and corrosion rates.
The initial material has a lamellar or interpenetrating microstructure containing at least two phases.
The constituent phases differ in electrochemical potential and corrosion response.
The relevant elevated-temperature interval is 450–650 °C.
A molten chloride salt is a relevant corrosive environment for the proposed test.
An acidic solution at 450–650 °C is an alternative relevant test environment.
Wear repeatedly removes protective oxide films that form on the relatively noble phase.
Wear-induced exposure of fresh surfaces increases effective interaction between phases with different electrochemical behavior.
Micro-galvanic coupling accelerates selective dissolution of one phase in a dual-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy.
Mechanical damage weakens interphase interfaces.
The multiphase eutectic alloy will have a higher total degradation rate than a composition-matched homogenized single-phase baseline.
The multiphase alloy will exhibit greater wear because of deeper pits and enhanced material removal at phase boundaries.
The multiphase alloy will exhibit a higher corrosion rate than the homogenized baseline because of localized galvanic attack.
Homogenizing the same or a closely matched composition into a predominantly single phase suppresses interphase galvanic effects.
A controlled comparison can use identical overall compositions processed into multiphase eutectic and predominantly single-phase states, followed by identical simultaneous wear-corrosion tests.
Total loss, wear-track volume, electrochemical metrics, and phase-selective damage are measurable responses capable of comparing the two states.
Failure of the multiphase samples to show significantly greater degradation in both wear and corrosion metrics than the single-phase baseline would falsify the proposed explanation.
